And if again the god himself had questioned them — "Do you then agree that you trust the Athenians on your own behalf more than yourselves?" — there could surely be no denying it. For they did not bring in a part to the common stock, but the whole contribution from all became a part of the city's own. And indeed they contributed such good courage and daring that to surpass so far in ships was a small thing. For alone of all mankind they endured to abandon their own city, that they might not look on while that of all the rest was made desolate; and alone, suffering this not at the hands of enemies, they removed themselves out by their own act for the sake of victory — not in misfortune at the hands of others, but they turned to virtue the very things that to others seem the limit of misfortunes in war, and took from Xerxes his hopes so far as concerned themselves, showing that even if ten thousand times he should hold the land, and search out the hearths, and tear up everything from the foundations, he would none the more cast down the dignity of the Athenians, nor take from them the being Athenians, but would labour at endless things, like the condemned in Hades. And yet what eagerness more brilliant, what good courage more manifest, will appear to one who examines what Greeks — or, to put it absolutely, what men? They gave up the land that they might be slaves neither on land nor on sea, reckoning that to keep what they had was the beginning of slavery, and making the loss of what they had a starting-point of goods to come; and they saved those who had their own from the very things by which they had given up their own. Such, then, was their eagerness before the dangers and toward the dangers — so unreasoning, so to speak, or, to say what is truer, so reasonable. And their conduct during the very contest and danger was so conspicuous that to them alone it may be said they conquered by themselves; for they were the first to make the rout.

But I wish to go back a little and to say something further before the sea-battle. For all others praise the multitude of the ships and the eagerness of the city and her deeds; but I — even if it is strange to say it — assert that they have all left out one thing, no less worthy than these to see and to admire, which I will now myself set in the midst, not ashamed of the truth. For whoever passes this over out of shame, and does so out of goodwill toward the city, acts much as if he should pass over the sea-battle out of goodwill toward the city. For the men of that day won both victories most clearly of all mankind, both having long dwelt in Athens and having recovered her still more nobly: for their enemies they conquered with arms, and their friends with their fairness. For consider: men who furnished so great eagerness for the safety of all, who paid in so great a contribution to the common need, who were everything — the affairs depending on the sea and the ships, those in the ships on the city, and the rest, as in a stormy season, taking refuge in their power and riding at anchor upon their virtue and fortune — and who, as I said, could not themselves have denied that this was so: that such men should add so much gentleness and greatness of spirit as to concede the leadership in name to others, and not to contend, nor, for the sake of things which even the dullest in nature would have claimed, and which others on their behalf, having no voice at all, would not so much as utter or hesitate over — how does this not show that all wisdom was truly with those men, and that they were the best of all men, whether one examine them by nations or by individuals or in any way whatever? For if they then, vexed at such folly, had stood aside or turned to contention, what device of safety, what good dream would have been left to the rest, or

what use of more or fewer ships would still have been there for the Greeks in their need? For come, by the gods — that we may dwell a little upon the discourse and that one may see more clearly their character and all that I am saying — suppose they had then asked the leadership of the Greeks, saying that, if they were defeated in the sea-battle, they would not be free to choose their own leaders, nor would the barbarian let them have any say over those who should rule among them, but they would have to follow him shamefully and become slaves and prey — and perhaps not even to follow, but, made to vanish in whatever manner seemed good to him, to depart from among men, with their temples and arms and laws; and saying that "we, foreseeing this, have changed our whole city into triremes, and, whether one must dare the greatest things, the common things of human nature have been given up by us on your behalf, or whether one must so equip oneself, since it is unlivable to be defeated, we have resolved on this; and to us alone victory is necessary; so that, whether you need anything of victory, so much has been already accomplished for you by us, or whether the contribution too must be considered, we alone fill two parts of the whole, and these but a twentieth of what comes from us" — if they had said this and added these heads, that "if you accept on these terms, well; but if not, consider whether you will not be depriving us of greater things than yourselves"; and if indeed they had added — for I leave aside the leader, who so far surpassed all that he was one in place of all, who alone, like a seer, expounded places and seasons and the secrets of the barbarians and what was to come — but if they had added to the challenge this only, that "if you have determined otherwise, another will gladly give us your leadership and add Median money and gifts; in view of which, choose whichever you wish" — would they have spoken either things not in keeping with justice, or such as the present necessities allowed one to overlook, if

they had used these arguments? For surely not — when the sea alone was left, and they were furnishing so many ships of their own, and were the head of the hopes, and stood at the turning-point of safety, and were the only fighters worthy of the affair, and had put themselves forward before all, in the rank not only of leaders but of fathers, and held, so to speak, the leadership from the very things they were doing — but suppose, on the contrary, that all things were common, and that no one excelled anyone, and that all contributed equally, and that the admirals were alike in their natures to one another, and it was a common fund, and one had to consider from what was available and appoint those who should lead: how could those men not shine through all like stars? Or how could they not, by the votes, be above all together, and not only by their skill? And yet this seems the least of just claims in such matters. For surely it was not the case that, on each single trireme, the steersmen ruled them, chosen for their craft, but that the leadership of them all was owed not to those most skilled in these things — but this too was a small part of the justice on their side. But this at least is plain, and alone sufficient: that, when some of those gathered had to lead the war against the barbarian, ought not those who alone, in the face of the former expedition of these same barbarians, faced danger on behalf of all — ought not these to lead? For those to whom the present was common with the rest who shared it, these conquered all by their own private deeds; and they would have received so much the smaller favour, by as much as they had freed all and were going to lead in the present matters.

And indeed, if no one gainsaid them in this, but all with both hands withdrew, how is it not worthy to admire their greatness of spirit? — who in every way overlooked their own concerns, and, having raised themselves so high before, yet again at that time, being ambitious beyond nature, sought nothing more. But if the Greeks were not going to heed them, and in anger abandoned them, what was there, in the midst of a Greece not even taken from her among the barbarians, to keep her from being admired — yet not even to have a name left now? But indeed

one of three things was necessary: either, all yielding, to hold the leadership — than which one could name no greater proof of their virtue and of their freeing the Greeks for nothing; or, none conceding this, all to perish, left in the lurch; or, for the votes to come out divided, in which case there was civil strife and war against one another, with no resource against the barbarians — a thing which, while it came about by the nature of the matter, is seen to have been prevented by their forethought. And indeed, if these things which I have just gone through were moving them, and they then kept their reckonings in silence, they offered a test of the utmost endurance. But if they thought themselves in no way the losers, whom is it worthy to set in the same rank with them, who knew how to be angry at the barbarians alone? But I think they arranged everything for this one end: to rescue both those present and those absent, the one willing, the other unwilling, and they saw this alone to be just; since, if they had examined everything purely, no Greek would then have been at Salamis. For I will add Salamis for the sake of good omen. But as it was, they judged this enough for themselves — that the affairs of the Greeks should be set right. And on this account they gave up not only the leadership, but the city itself, preferring the common interest to all private security and advantage, and reckoning that they would truly accomplish a great leadership, if they should lead the Greeks toward freedom and safety. And the Lacedaemonians, like men teaching children beforehand, they wished to make more eager. And on this account they led them out in front, for the sake of exhortation and that they might imitate what was being done by themselves. And these things they did even in their decrees. Yet they did not, as in word and in the wing of the line of battle, so also in deeds yield the leadership to others — far from it; but the one party furnished the name of leaders, the other the deeds, and the figure was set so much the nobler for them, in proportion as they held leadership over the leaders

themselves. For whatever did not seem good to a single one of the Athenians was all void; so that the Lacedaemonian admiral ruled the commanders from each people, but the Athenian ruled a ruler of commanders. And the Greeks, seeing this for themselves, gave the prize of the sea-battles to the city, and furnished the testimony of those truly present and eyewitnesses as to who had led them toward safety. And it befell the city to bear off the first honours from two sides at once. For among cities Athens excelled, and among men one man, an Athenian. Thus what was a matter of gentleness of character they showed in conceding; and what belonged to a true leadership was assigned to those men by all. And indeed, for the rest of the war, the Greeks now set the city purely at their head; for all the gatherings and councils, from this time on, were toward the Athenians and from the Athenians, and the city became the common council-chamber of the war against the barbarian.

But the zeal about the demonstrations, and one argument handing us on to another, has carried us too far. I return again to the very deeds, since I have set out in the midst the things I wished. And let no one think that we are spending more time than is needed, or taking up again things already worked out; but let him consider how great is the need, and the occasion of each part of the discourse, and where it tends. And if he considers thus, the things said will seem many, but each to be said once for all; and that by necessity they are all rivals, so that one cannot leave anything out without slighting it, but that by their arrangement they cannot fall otherwise; and what for the moment seems a digression he will know to belong to the continuity and the sequence, taking these things up in his own mind and considering whether they might somehow fit better otherwise. And further: if we were making this examination and zeal about matters of no worth, or about those whose examples are taken from next door, one might reasonably

say we were splitting hairs; but as it is, concerning matters about which all the poets, in speaking, have fallen short, and all the power of words has been worsted, and all men, as if from amazement, marvel rather than those who have seen each thing in exactness — concerning these we contend a contest in words little less than those men contended in deeds at that time. It is fitting, then, to leave nothing idle or unexamined, since alike the zeal over small things brings blame and the failing, in matters so great, to preserve the worth throughout. For this too one might say is, in another fashion, the act of a hairsplitter. But I return.

For when the disaster at Thermopylae had befallen, and Greece had been opened up brilliantly and perilously, some poured in like men breaking through the gates of a wall, robbed of neither of two divisions. For some willingly, some by necessity, went over, as the war flooded round and all in succession fled before it like an oncoming fire; but those who in many cases and often had already shown that they are rightly named after Athena, and use the goddess's mind very graciously, and were conscious that the city's guard lay outside, make a decree: to entrust the city to the city-holding goddess, to place their children and wives in safekeeping at Troezen, and themselves, stripped of superfluities, to put forward the sea — furnishing, on a single day, all the things one might call greatest among men as tokens of piety, endurance, prudence, humanity, greatness of spirit: of piety, through the trust they had in the gods; of endurance, severed from their children and wives and the company of their nearest, with hearts that bore it; of humanity, because they endured these things for the safety of others. And indeed, for greatness of spirit, who of men is like to those who gave up their possessions for freedom? But indeed to know the one thing that was going to preserve all their affairs —

wisdom, I mean — through which they surpassed all who ever were even in that obedience to rulers which is honoured by all in words, by their resolution. And they, thus stripped for action, held the Greeks at Salamis; while he was at hand with both hands, leading the Greeks up to Attica together with the barbarians, and sends again to Salamis, ordering what he had before, to take earth and water, thinking that, if the talk came while the terrors were present and seen, they would somewhat the more be bent and would lend an ear; and there he was most of all cheated of his hope. For so far were they from fear, or from changing their minds about what had been resolved from the beginning, that when someone dared to say they ought to yield, the men themselves, and the women falling upon the woman, destroyed them out of hand. And this was the first exhortation toward the sea-battle that came to the Greeks, common to the men and the women. Nor did they shame it by their deeds in what followed; but first, when the Greeks were deliberating things unworthy of the daring at Artemisium and of the Athenian presence, and flight was already winning, they themselves prevented it and forced them, like unwilling children, to stand firm, working everything by their attendance — at first persuading them, who scarcely admitted a word; then, since it was endless, unexpectedly laying necessity upon them and contriving the sea-battle, so that they took courage perforce. Then, when the meeting was made and the barbarians had covered with their ships all the space outside, then, being shut out of land and sea by just so much as the triremes occupied, and truly, as on the sea and amid waves, seeing the same thing on every side wherever they looked — enemies — they yielded to others in nothing, but were themselves the first to begin the sea-battle, as in Euboea

so too here, when all the others hung back, they alone wrought the whole. Whatever, by a general's forethought, had to be done beforehand to harm the king — so as to find friends and fellow-suppliants for victory among the enemy (I mean the affair concerning the Ionians) — that they prepared; and what had to be done by the law of hands and with common good courage, this they both dared and accomplished most nobly of all under the sun as witness, ranging themselves opposite to those who were the head of the enemy's fleet, and being the first to rout and to destroy the ships in every kind of action, here and there, and leaving the rest to pursue rather than to fight a sea-battle. So that to me the Greeks seem to have won that sea-battle much as if, present at Marathon too, they had shared in the victory. For there the city sufficed for herself, and at Salamis the rest enjoyed what was done. And then the Lacedaemonians came a single day too late for the battle; on that day the contributors came too late even for the rout. And so great is the difference, that one might reasonably say the Greeks justly owe the city thanks not only for their freedom and for the prizes of the sea-battle, but for the victory itself. For they appear to have taken this too as some additional gain, and to have shared in the ambition in common. There then every beach was full of wrecks, all the straits were confounded, and the passage carried out to the mainland for the king dreadful sights, very much out of tune with his cleverness and luxury. And it is fitting to make mention also of the addition to the evils that befell the barbarians. For the by-work of the deeds was wrought out as no less honourable. What, then, was this? Three places the barbarians had seized at the outset — the mainland, the sea, the island before

Salamis — so that the Greeks might be shut in more exactly than by a net. For it seems a great calamity, even contrary to the Median law, if any of those who dared to lift their hand against the king should escape. Against those, then, who were cast out of the sea-battle, the chief part of the army was stationed — the foremost men of the Persians — and they held the island, standing by as though over a sure prey. But when they failed of the first prizes, and fortune was with the Greeks and the trial had turned about, one Athenian man undertook the danger willingly, and taking those of them who were on Salamis, the older men, and landing them on the island, kills all this Persian force. And Xerxes sat upon the mainland in his array, as though making some other contest, or as one of the judges from heaven of what was happening, thinking that the fear of him would suffice for his own men. And the deed was for him only so great as to be angry at some of his soldiers and to honour others. But when he saw the sea boiling with blood and surge, and everything full of corpses and wrecks, and others more masterful frightening both his men and himself, struck with terror and thinking the city a wonder-worker, he sang a recantation, and turning back, went the same road — not with the same array, now making this one thing his contest, to reach the bridge.

Thus through all the city saved the whole Greek race, and was shown to all to be the only safeguard for the Greeks — and, I think, for the rest of the inhabited world as well. By what marks do I say "to all"? By those in which she conquered before alone at Marathon; by those in which afterward she so far outwent her fellow-combatants; by those in which she herself was the head of the war in both expeditions; by those who failed at Thermopylae without the city, and those who won at Artemisium through the city; by the oracles of the god, some of which said the gift was Athena's, others that the Greeks would perish if the Athenians sided

with the barbarians. So that from what the Greeks did not suffer and from what they were going to suffer, from what the city did and what she alone did not do, she carries off the judgment of the whole; and besides this, by the contribution of her general, by the multitude of her triremes, by beginning the sea-battles, by finding the places, by holding the Greeks together, by being the first to conquer the greatest part of the fleet, by destroying the most, by the apparitions from Eleusis, by the extra deeds at Psyttaleia, by the witness of her foes. For the one party gave the prize of valour to the city, and gave that she should lead in matters where she already led; and their king fled away. So that from gods and from men, from friends and from foes, the votes were given to the city. And to her, again, these things come from two sides: some from what was approved and accomplished in common, some from what was done through the general. And the king's affairs stood thus; but Mardonius was left behind, longing for death, conscious that he had been in part responsible for the expedition, and resolving on something even from this same staying and fortune — having dared, and having received from the king the best of the foot, he sat down before them. Yet not even for these things did the Greeks need others, but, as though it were one further thing left, the city wrought this out too, and went through to the very end, like men plaiting garlands. The others, then, take pride in their share of the battle, all who indeed were present — and these not coming near the city in size of camp or in eagerness; but your city won again, long before the battle, both Mardonius and the king, in a victory truly her own and belonging to the Athenians alone. For when all the Greek race looked to her, and it had been well recognized by both sides where the masters of affairs lay — both by the Greeks, I mean, and by the barbarians — a thought comes to the king and to Mardonius, which one may call both shrewd and silly

at once. The strongest course of all was plainly this, if it had succeeded; but this was, more than anything, impossible. And what was this? They planned to bring the city over to themselves and to strip her of her Greek character — not only conscious of the past, but seeing the present too, that it was through her that things were led; and besides, the oracles from Delphi, as it is said, expressly bore witness that, if the Athenians should join with them, the affairs of the Greeks would be gone. It seemed good, then, to the king — both buying off his fear and bethinking him of the gain — to make trial of the city; and he sends heralds saying the opposite of before. For in place of the earth and water he had asked before, these things he now offered — and not on an equal measure, but on the one hand he gave them back their city and all their land, on the other he added the rest of Greece as a gift. And apart from these, there was money beyond all that was among the Greeks, and to be his friends and allies securely; from which he testified that he both feared them alone and trusted them alone, more than all he had, if he could persuade them. And the sum of the embassy was such. And the herald was Alexander, king of Macedonia. But they were so far from admiring the promises, or from thinking that even if he gave all he possessed he was worthy of them, that the office of public-guest saved the ambassador. Nor even so did they send him off altogether without fear, but warned him that, unless he were beyond their borders before sunset, and that for the future he should be public-guest of some others rather than the Athenians, since such embassies could not be brought without death; and at the same time guides led him through the land, so that none should touch him or speak with him. This answer I hold no less worthy of admiration than the sea-battle at Salamis and the trophies, and to afford no less ambition either to those who gave it or to him
who persuaded them. For in those things they had to make use also of arms and triremes and engines, but here they used their own pure selves, judgment and word.

What contestants of virtue, then, are nobler, or who of all that ever were made a more lasting display of it? — who continued unconquered by gold and silver and iron and all things, and made everything alike useless to the king, as though it were still hidden beneath the earth, honouring poverty above wealth, choosing dangers above security, and justice above so great a humanity from the king. And it was not that they were thus hostile and arrayed against the barbarian promises, but submissive to the Greek ones, if there were added the show of need, or, so far at least as to give them a longer hearing. But when the Lacedaemonians came in great fear and begged the opposite of the king's embassy, promising to feed their children and old men and women for them so long as the war lasted, they pardoned rather than accepted it — counting them good through fear, but in their offers still inexperienced of the Athenians; and they showed their greatness of spirit no less by restraining their anger than by thrusting away the offers. For, being made by nature to do good and not to receive it, they knew that they themselves owed a wage to those who do good to the Greek race, and not that they should receive from others a wage for their virtue, nor love for gain those who gave themselves up — no more than one loves children and parents for gain — but should save them even at expense, as is fitting for those whose minds are disposed as toward their own. And this so great deed shone forth for the account of virtue in the seasons of the war, between the sea-battle at Salamis and the battle at Plataea. And again from these things, apart from what I went through before, both the king and the Greeks, in everything, set the Athenians foremost — the one calling them to his side through Mardonius, the others begging them not to do these things through

the Lacedaemonians. For the dragging on both sides and the calling of each party to themselves was a plain vote and clear pledge from both, that they were conscious that the Athenians were stronger, by no little, than themselves and than their adversaries. And having hoped thus from the beginning, they departed admiring still more; for the one party they did not endure, the other they received with much superiority. So that the likely thing too was added: that they themselves should cast their own worthy vote on their own behalf, and that there should be three witnesses in succession — the enemies, the allies, and themselves, having shown themselves alike in deed throughout. And gathering the Greeks, who could now better follow them, they come to Plataea. And the dignity of the camps, or the array of the barbarians, as it was ranged through Boeotia, or the things before the battle, to relate is a waste not reaching to the matter's worth. But again a wonderful testimony is given to the city by both sides at the battle. For the Lacedaemonians yielded to the Athenians the post against the Persians, as though it were allotted by some necessity and by nature that the Persians should be conquered by the Athenians. And again Mardonius led the Lacedaemonians round against himself, choosing them in exchange, thinking it more to his profit that the Lacedaemonians should die nobly than that the Athenians should conquer nobly; for he found this from the examples concerning themselves. So, as boxers first contend for their stance, they on the one hand received the Persians, on the other received all men, and were, in all, victorious — the barbarians by valour, the Greeks by valour and by numbers. And they decide the battle, going through all, and destroying the leaders of the horse. And when there was need of an assault on the wall, the others were toward them only so far as one would be ashamed to say, until of the barbarians some no longer held Boeotia as before, lying low,

while others, as though from a shipwreck, unarmed and out of order, holding the night more precious than the day, withdrew, few from many, and the many in small bands, with much memory of the proud army and of the Athenians. When matters had come to this, all the other Greeks gladly drew breath, having escaped a storm beyond what they had even expected, and crowned the city, and admired her, and held whatever they might say of her too small. So far were they from being able to do anything that should seem worthy of her; and she here, most of all, displayed the abundance of her virtue. For she went so far in the matter as to show the barbarians still more, outside Greece, who they were that had done these things to them within Greece, and from whom, having judged it a good thing to flee, they departed.

I see, then, that the discourse is being stretched out, and that after such things as have been said it is not easy either to speak with any pleasure, or to find hearers — like another contestant entering after one already well-approved. Yet I undertook these speeches not for the sake of charm so much as to show, with truth, the worth of the city; so that I shall do wrong by leaving off rather than weary by speaking. Then one must reflect, even from the very symbol of the speeches, that we are not bound to measure even the feast of the Panathenaia itself by a single day, but — if this too must be added — the multitude of days has been set aside for ornament and solemnity; so that neither is the multitude of words out of season in such a season of deeds. We know, surely, that the gymnastic contest, and still more the musical one, is not bounded once for all, but ends, so to speak, on each day and again begins from the beginning, and is not filled out by the kinds of spectacle on a single day. So that whatever escapes the present occasion has not, at any rate, passed by the whole festival. Or it would be altogether absurd,

if the lawgivers extended their gatherings for this very reason — and, by Zeus, even overstepped the very name of the sacred month, adding more time, that we might be in one another's company as long as possible — and we, instead of using this, should find fault. As, then, we are not vexed at meeting the exercises of the games day by day, but enjoy as a gain the spectacle ever present, so it is fitting to feel about the speeches too — and these too among the things allotted to the festival; assuredly you will not meet with things always stale among what is left over, nor commune with things less honourable than those.

But, that I may not, in begging off beyond what is necessary, lengthen by this very thing, I will turn now to the next and continuous part of the speeches. For when Greece had become her own again and all had departed — ships, horses, the foot, satraps, king — first there were festivals and processions to the gods such as no one remembers to have taken place either before or after in a free Greece. For it was not a law that gathered them, nor a fixed cycle of time, but out of the events themselves it was given to each man and to cities to be of good cheer and to wear garlands and to call the gods to witness the happiness at hand. And on the one hand an altar of Zeus the Deliverer was set up — a thank-offering to the god himself and a memorial to those who had succeeded, on the very spot of the deeds, carrying a common exhortation to the Greeks both to concord and to despise the barbarians; on the other, the common shrine of the Greeks at Delphi was adorned with fair and fitting inscriptions, and the cities took on not only the ornament that comes from virtue, but also that from building, and the wealth of the barbarians was distributed among the better men. And indeed here too the city will appear to have excelled by as much as in the very deeds. For first

she adorned the acropolis with memorials of the deeds, and added to the beauty of nature a rival ornament from wealth and art, so that the whole was, in place of a dedication — or rather in place of a statue. And next she hung up other honours for the gods, beyond all Greek power, some at home, some abroad; and she herself passed her ancient bounds in every direction, worthily of the deeds, and made an addition to her circuit. To put it briefly, she alone was made uninhabited through virtue, and she alone, out of virtue, was inhabited again and took on what was before uninhabited, becoming, in deeds and glory and ornament, fairer and greater. But here I have fallen, as it were unwillingly, along the road of the discourse rather than by foresight; for it was not toward these things that I was hastening, but I wished to show this: that if the fairest thing for men, and at the same time the most profitable and that which conquers in pleasure, is the visits and converse of the gods, and this then blossomed to so great a height among the Greeks, one would most justly assign it to this one city — first by reason of the honour of the gods truly itself; for we all repay the gods as the causes of our goods, and the city appears to have been, of what then came to men, in the highest degree the cause of what resulted; and next by so far excelling in the very dedications and thank-offerings. For these symbols of her piety are proofs of beauty and greatness. Yet she did not think this enough — to give thanks to the gods for what had happened and to seek nothing further, nor to sit upon her trophies, as though distrusting herself; but, judging her present possessions a stepping-stone to what was to come, she contended against herself, deliberating nobly and as befitted the occasion: for in the second times she thought fit to do the second things. And these were

to march out in turn against those who had first made war upon her, and to remove the fears and the dangers into their country. And this is most worthy of admiration among those deeds — the figure of the war and its constitution. For of two other kinds of war — the one, if one begins from the beginning; the other, if one defends oneself — the former is not attended by justice, while from the latter the addition of necessity takes away the ambition, since by nature deliberate choice is separated from necessity. Now, I think, the one who does what is just under necessity is better than the one who transgresses willingly; yet not the whole, so to speak, becomes his own. And so then the disgrace of the former war fell upon the barbarians, and what was owed met them from the Greeks; so that they had conquered, but the part that comes of abundance was not present. But what one might call a third figure of war — to march out in turn against those who first plotted, using the freedom of those who begin and the justice of those who defend — this, then, the city resolved to show the barbarians, both on her own behalf and on behalf of the other Greeks: that it does not rest with them, when they come, to make the Greeks brave, nor that these things were done by them through chance and necessity, but because they thought it not honourable for the others to rule first; "and now, when rule has come round to the rank of the just, you will know well and nobly whom you have stirred up." Thus I say that, for a demonstration of justice and of true courage, the second deeds — that I may say nothing offensive — were wrought by the city no less clearly than the former. And besides this, she reckoned that the safety and preservation of the Greeks lay not in keeping them shut up at their hearth, nor in doing nothing either through them or themselves on their own behalf, but in thrusting the barbarians as far as possible from Greece; so she thought there would be the best and purest peace for all — reckoning rightly and seeing things as they are by nature. For nearly those alone are purely at peace who have shown that they are not at all in need of keeping peace.

Such was the reasoning of the city, containing all that one might call fairest in human nature. Having so resolved — and what should I say first, or what last? — they won the battle at Mycale by no small margin, and searched the coasts of Europe, in case any of the invaders were still hidden, and drove some from the Strymon, some from Sestos, some from Byzantium. They went over all, purging it as it were of pollution, and they cast anchor no less than men sailing on trade. And the journey of Triptolemus, told to have been through the air, in the part where he had left off, they imitated. For he, doing good to all in common; they, going against those from whom vengeance had to be taken, punishing — thinking that this too profited the common race of mankind, to bring the insolent and those who think beyond their nature to fitting penalties. Having so resolved, at once they sailed round Asia, and at once they sailed up by the receiving rivers, and at once they were heard, at once they were seen; and they displayed a wonderful and truly armed war-dance. So densely and intensely did they rush upon the matters that even the Lacedaemonians, present at the first of the deeds, then departed, as men unable to follow the winged. And this same thing those of the other Greeks too who had first sailed out with them did — they grew dizzy and departed; while those who held the men from Asia, whom the king had before led against them and Greece, these they used as sufficient. And the king's own affairs were a starting-point for them against the king. For roadsteads and walls and stockades and everything received them, and arms and ships became theirs. And they left no part of their own virtue untried, fighting at sea, at once against Phoenicians and Cilicians and Cyprians in the midst of the Egyptian sea and capturing whole fleets, and at the same moment against the whole Persian

empire risking themselves on land, destroying and capturing numbers of nations in place of a number of bodies. And already two trophies came in one day, and a sea-battle was matched with a land-battle. And they so surpassed the king that they made his empire and its places more renowned by their victories. The Eurymedon, at any rate, is sung not least because of these men. And they showed that one need not cross by yoking the straits with a flax-bound raft, nor wrestle against the highest of the mountains, as though it were something nobler, but, excelling in courage and judgment, prevail everywhere — with the fairest provisions of all, I think, and purely from home; for these alone, of what men have, are theirs through to the end, while the rest lie common before all, so to speak, gifts of fortune — or, if you will, of virtue. For they belong to the worse too from the beginning, but they are kept, reasonably, by the better. So they tested the whole empire, and shook it, and brought matters to such a pass — those enrolled in the Persian to such contempt, and the city to such confidence in all toward her — that the Libyans about Pharos were stirred, the Egyptians revolted along with them, and the king, though he seemed to fare in the rest as he wished concerning them, lost no small part of Egypt, the marsh-land — though before he had twice already taken all of it. And the matter of the triremes from Athens was like a kind of bolt from heaven. For alone of men who have lived in a commonwealth, they reckoned their own land as though it were another's, and another's land as not theirs, but as belonging to those who held it in wickedness. They lived the life of guards — and not of guards stationed in one place, nor patrols of some single spot, but those men one must call patrols of the whole Greek world; and they chose as enemies not the weakest, but those most able to endure the most, moved by two things: one, that nothing of the extreme — so far as concerns the judgment and preparation of the barbarians —

had been left undone to the Greeks but their not having suffered it, for which they must take vengeance, and in no small way; the other, that toward the rest of time there should be safety for Greece — until the king came to know that, in lifting his hand against the city, he was doing something like what one would do who, raised up against a great oncoming flame, wrestled with fuel. For there was nothing that he did not suffer, but he was consumed of himself, and perceived that he held the land as a fortress against his own safety; and he advanced upon the road, reckoning the third thing nobler than the first — or rather, more necessary. For at first he had desired to take Greece in addition, and the rest of Europe; but he perceived that he was in love with the impossible. Second was for him to preserve the empire he had; not even this did the city allow. He came to make safety itself the thing of greater worth, and he withdrew before the city by so much, from land and sea, not as the saying is "to back water," nor as to "give ground," but he gave up all the lower region, no fewer than myriads of stades of Asia — the whole being like a great empire — so that not only were the islands and the Greeks of every kind in them free, but those who dwelt in his own country were further from his dominion and rule than before were those of the old Greece. For he held before the region as far as the Peneus — and yet I have taken away the marvel, as though I were saying something marvellous; he held all as far as Attica, until he met those from Attica on the sea: so far had he passed the navel of the earth and of Greece, Delphi. But from the contests and expeditions of the city he came down to this, that he agreed to sail no longer within two bounds — setting the Chelidonian isles to the south and the Cyanean to the north — and to keep off the sea by five hundred stades on every side; so that this circle is, in place of any other, a crown above the head of the Greeks, and the king's guard set up from his own country.

Such was the war the city made against the barbarians, both on her own land and in theirs; and such, again, the peace she made, showing by both that it was not in pursuit of wealth, nor for the pleasure of gain, that she went on, but hunting this one thing: secure freedom for the Greeks from the barbarians. And yet what fairer chief-point of peace or of war could one name, whether against Greeks or against barbarians, than that with which the city then sealed her deeds? And these so many and such things she went through with many oppositions from the Greeks, all as it were pulling against her — the Lacedaemonians standing aloof in purpose, the Boeotians warring against her, the Aeginetans fighting against her at sea (whom one thing kept from being first at sea — the city, by far the victor); and besides these, the Corinthians stirred up through the Megarians and warring both by land and by sea, the Epidaurians and Sicyonians being counted with the Corinthians, the Naxians and Thasians and Carystians ill-advised about the alliance, the Phocians calling, the Lacedaemonians again calling, and a wonderful circle of affairs throughout Greece; so that, even if these alone had sufficed and we had only her Greek deeds of that time to relate, with no Median splendours present anywhere, they would suffice to fill the years for a narrative. For which one must especially rejoice with the city, not only for her strength, but for her greatness of spirit; for that, while at war and in rivalry of the Greeks against her, she gave up none the more her forethought on behalf of the Greeks, but warred against the king on behalf of the common interests through all land and sea — how great a greatness of spirit must one add to this? Apart from being so divided and reaching all things as if each alone — to furnish, of judgment, courage; and of

preparation, surpassing measure, for one to admire? For she so ordered her affairs against the barbarians, as one having all leisure from all else, and to those of the Greeks who troubled her it was no more possible to make use of the occasion, but she met these too in such a way as to be able to count off these victories, five and more together, like other things reckoned all at once. They conquered the Peloponnesians at sea off Cecryphaleia; they conquered the Aeginetans off Aegina, and the Peloponnesians again. For the Megarians they set up walls down to the sea, and at once preserved their freedom and their land; they conquered the Corinthians before Megara, and before twelve days had passed they conquered them again in another battle, when they were ignobly snatching away the trophy. And these things are not yet great; but it shall be told, even though I am pressed — for the addition will show the whole. For the powers of the city were away: the one for the need of the Egyptians, ships more than then were all the ships among the Greeks together, well-nigh; the other was set down before Aegina — which the more stirred their adversaries to set out for Megara. For they thought there was leisure of the Athenians for the deed against themselves; and if even the second engagement should be won, then she would have to break off another siege, that of Aegina, for there was no other place from which they would come henceforth. But these so laughed the sophism to scorn that the men at Aegina were no more moved than those in Egypt who had heard nothing, but the rest of the age — the oldest and the youngest — go to the help of Megara, and in two battles in succession appeared stronger than the prime of the Corinthians and Peloponnesians; so that those men now exactly conceded, and had nothing more to say, not even that they had not justly added these present things. And it seems to me that, by the goodwill and zeal of some god toward the city, this second affair was contrived, as in

a drama. For if they had departed as men struck once, there might perhaps have been some later rejoinder for them; but to be reproached by their own people, and, reproached, to go out again, and, setting up a trophy greater than the former, to add to their suffering — this made them themselves set their seal upon the victory, so that the deed should not seem to be judged by fortune rather than by the account of the better, both now and before. So they did not make trial of a third — though they themselves forced the contestants together at the Isthmus.

Are these things, then, all we can tell of those men? Surely we should rob them of many great things. They sailed round the Peloponnese — not to speak of it simply as naval circumnavigations, but so as to master the strategic points of the country, and to defeat in trifling fashion those who stood against them, general after general. They crossed to the opposite mainland, all that they met giving way. Again, when the Lacedaemonians came over against the Phocians, the Crisaean gulf was closed, and they met them at the borders. And apart from these, before Megara, they were in Geraneia; so that the Lacedaemonians had no resource, but were at a loss, standing among the Boeotians, where they might be saved: so did the city enfold them. And at last they engage at Tanagra in Boeotia, and when both proved men worthy of the daring, the Lacedaemonians seemed in this one point to have had the better — how shall I say it becomingly? For I shrink from saying that they were not destroyed. For this was the limit: for the Athenians, to close the pass; for the Lacedaemonians, to be saved home. And this deed comes near to being the only one in which flight has been a symbol of victory, since those who in the battle too were the stronger, and in the whole, without many of the earlier proofs, the things that followed at once showed. For there are three witnesses who attested on the spot that the victory was the Athenians':

Athenians, Lacedaemonians, Boeotians. For the Lacedaemonians were content to withdraw, the Athenians went forward hard upon the battle, and the Boeotians did not hold out, but, beaten at Oenophyta, bowed down, and with them the Phocians and Locrians, by a single victory. And from these the city took this penalty in return for their having sided with the barbarian in the common dangers of Greece. And there is another deed of hers worth telling, and this too shouting and showing aloud from afar whose it was. For when the earthquake about Laconia took place, and the perioikoi stood round the Lacedaemonians, and all the affairs in the Peloponnese were truly shaken as in an earthquake, the Lacedaemonians had no sooner called than the people was at hand under arms — bold in courage, but full of fear on their behalf as on behalf of its own safety; which both dissolved the present terrors for Lacedaemon and made ready to take vengeance on them hereafter. So nowhere is it possible to embrace the deeds or the darings of the city more than the character of her deeds, which marks the doers more exactly than a trophy. The expedition for the Milesians, and the sea-battles off Samos, and the chastened revolt of the Euboeans, and many other things, one may indeed pass over. And at last, having mastered all, she makes a peace worth recalling. For she did not make her treaty in the same manner toward the Greeks as toward the barbarians, but reversed it. For from those she took away all the lower country and the sea within the bounds I mentioned; but to the Greeks, what she had become mistress of in the war, this she gave back — Megara, Troezen, Pegae, all Achaea. By which it is clear that she made the peace while in the position of victor; for there was nothing she received in return, but she brought forth one and the same as a symbol of two things, both of surpassing in the war and of her inborn goodness — holding that against the barbarians one must war to

the utmost of one's power, but against the Greeks simply up to the point of superiority. Having so carried through the contest against the barbarians, and so again the contest against the Greeks, such a peace she made toward those, and such toward these, becoming superior to both together and apart. And indeed she alone of all cities, by her own dangers, procured a benefit common to the whole race; and she alone, out of common benefactions, acquired the leadership and altered the custom. For it was not from enslaving the cities that she got her rule, but from making them free; so that it came about that the same time brought to the Greeks the gain of freedom, and to the city the gain of rule. For they alone ruled the willing, and this people alone, like a single ruler chosen out of all, prevailed — forcing the barbarians with arms, and not persuading their kindred, but persuaded by them to rule, holding rule as a symbol of justice, not of injustice. And if one must put it with a distinction, she alone of cities got her rule with the barbarians unwilling, the Greeks asking for it.

When matters had thus advanced, for a while there was quiet, and the cities enjoyed the happiness they had; but of the common fortune of men, which moves all things, both the Greeks and the city had their share. For the one party did not keep gratitude through to the end for the good they had received, but envied the excesses of her deeds; and she, against those for whom she had undergone everything, clashed — showing by two things how unwillingly: by at first restraining them while they were still being stirred, and asking that the differences be judged by argument; and by, when forced to war, seeking nothing more when she had conquered, but letting go those who had contended with her about the leadership, and leading them out of prison no more unpleasantly than

she had thrown them in at the beginning when she prevailed. But what should one make of these things now? For I am ashamed even to leave out the sea-battles at Naupactus, which they won by no small margin and against no slightly greater numbers, but sailing as upon a windfall; and other victories on the Thracian coast, and how they rescued Corcyra, and the deeds about Ambracia, the greatest of the Greek deeds of that time — and these done by virtue, not by need; and the things at Pylos itself, sea-battles from land and land-battles afterward on the island; and, before these were done, other Lacedaemonians brought from Cythera, and trophies of Corinthians, and many other things, rivals both to tell and to admire. But the occasion does not bear it; it seems to me a thing of greater good fortune to hold it in. And further, as we said, we did not undertake to relate what the city has done as a bare history — for then the discourse would stretch into the next quadrennial festival — but to tell the most renowned of her deeds in the wars, and of the goods belonging to the city to leave out nothing, so far as possible. And these things consist not in our telling each thing through all, but in our leaving out no kind of praise. And as it seemed good to the deity that these things should not yet suffice for Greece, but that the cities should still be tossed both by land and by sea, and that some enemies should come from abroad, while others sailed abroad in their misfortunes — what Greek or what barbarian is there who could name others equal to those from this city? To whom it occurred to sail for the freedom of the Leontines, and they thought fit to risk themselves for that of the Egestaeans, and they purposed to cross against the Carthaginians, in return for the Carthaginians' having first crossed against the Greeks in Sicily; and they manned triremes and merchantmen, as though sending them out from all Greece. And the land-battles and horse-battles are perhaps less to be amazed at, because of the city's constant habit of

conquering, and because the portion of the better has been given to the city as a kind of prize in most things; but that, even when affairs went against her, she fell away none the more, but — with hoplites absent, with cavalry absent, equal to whom in number or virtue it was impossible to find; and with so many ships and missiles and equipment and arts and allies and, so to speak, all her furnishing removed elsewhere, as though all Sicily were just then being colonized, the acropolis emptied of well-nigh ten thousand talents, the Lacedaemonians and Boeotians and the rest now making their invasions not from the Peloponnese but from the heart of Attica, from Decelea, and the household slaves having removed, no fewer than to seem the full complement of a nation, and with impunity for desertion to whoever wished, and so great a war about the city — that she should display so great an abundance of endurance and at once of strength and of ambition as to send out another expedition to match the former, and rival generals, and think fit to besiege the Lacedaemonians there with the alliance — to what human soul can one compare these things, and what good fortune should one not rather admire? And when the great disaster had come — for I will not be silent, but this too seems to me to show the city still greater — she bore herself toward the remaining affairs as though she had taken all Sicily. For she did not resemble one stripped of power, but one who had just acquired it. And the easiness of her ways and her moderation and the order of her conduct, which they chose for the sake of conceding nothing shameful, no one could worthily tell. And when all the Greeks stood round them, and their existing enemies then for the first time took hope and were spurred on by fortune, and those from Sicily came upon them, and the alliance changed, well-nigh all of it, and islands and mainland and all, so to speak, became enemies and surrounded them on every side, and an unexpected piece of folly besides came about, so that even the king was

called against the city by those who had been saved from him by the city's deeds — and he joined in, very gladly, and warred with bodies and ships and gold, and what starting-point of land or sea did he not furnish for the war? — there was no one who, looking on from outside, would not have expected the city to be snatched up now at last, held fast in so common a war of barbarians and Greeks; but they so turned matters about, as though all these things were for them, not against them, or as though the enemy were their own generals. And, greatest of all, when even the constitution was shaken and certain of those at home were estranged from them, having no place where they had to stand except Samos — as in the Median danger they had Salamis — but coming, these too, in some other fashion to the same point as those of that time, and abandoning the city in its greatest part, they set right matters at home and mastered those abroad and parted the Hellespont with trophies, pursuing some in one direction, some in another, as though making rather practice-exercises among themselves than sea-battles against those they met. (It has been said, and I considered it, that this has been said before by another.) And at last, falling in at Cyzicus together with the Lacedaemonians and the men from Greece and the barbarians from Asia and Pharnabazus, they take the ships, all but as many as they destroyed; and when Pharnabazus tried to heal the disaster and brought up his cavalry, the one party fighting from foot on horseback, the other from the ships, they overpower all at once — fleet, cavalry, the archers from Sicily, those from the Peloponnese, the king's provision, the hopes of the Lacedaemonians; and the war was now empty for their adversaries, and everything was gone, as truly as from a shipwreck. So that the city which had been so far surpassed by faction did not even conceive the name

of peace in those times, while those who set out from so many and so great advantages, when struck, took refuge at once in peace. I have always, for my part, blamed those who reproach the city of the Lacedaemonians and think fit to do this on behalf of yours; for they make themselves hateful to those, and do not, as they suppose, adorn you. But, if one must say something paradoxical, they seem to me to do the opposite of what they wish; for they exalt those men more than they praise the city, and I think more thanks would come to them from those men for the slander than from you for the praises. For those men are not penalized by being called second to the city, but gain by being judged against the city; while you they do not glorify by declaring you the stronger, but by the very setting-side-by-side they seem not to know you; so that it is not unlikely that you should feel more displeased than the Lacedaemonians, whenever they contend in this way.

But since I have come to be in this part of the discourse, in which the cities are compared with one another, it is necessary perhaps to endure this too, that we may show not only in the contests how much the stronger the city is, but in the whole. For the Lacedaemonians will appear to have lost three hundred men and not endured it, but to have given way at once — which gives the city greater ambition than to have won the battle; for in that she became superior to those who stood against her, but here she became superior in things in which the rest gave up, almost all, as in games, when everyone yields. But she, having had so great a disaster afterward in Sicily, not only did not cower, nor gladly take refuge in peace, but so disposed her enemies that they would gladly have seen anyone able to persuade the city to keep peace. And when they heard of Conon's siege in Mytilene, they were not dismayed, but, sailing to Arginusae with fewer ships than anyone would have guessed, fewer

nevertheless than their adversaries, they ranged themselves with their whole fleet against the enemy's, as though someone else always furnished them the triremes, and made their trials in the Carian rather than in their own bodies; and they took no thought either of the multitude of those arrayed against them, or of Callicratidas' reputation, or of islands held, or of fortune by now, so to speak, estranged; they were not beaten by the storm, nor did they take thought how much of the war was left, but, as though it were enough to look upon the sea, they rout the Lacedaemonians, master all the Peloponnesians, take some triremes and sink others, fighting at once against the thunderbolt and the enemy, and so changed the siege; and, greatest of all, they rescue the man who alone afterward sufficed to dissolve the dominion of the Lacedaemonians. And those, as though all conquered at sea, again begged for peace; so the city was wont then not only to conquer those present in the contests, but also to amaze the rest and to conquer through all. And indeed she will appear both to have won the greatest victories of any, and to have borne her misfortunes so that one would rather admire the city's good courage in dangers than the deeds of the conquerors; so that it occurs even to me to say this: that, conquering in her good fortunes, she has excelled no less in those in which she failed, since no one has borne misfortunes in like manner. Of her conquering in what she achieved — apart from what she did against those who opposed her in politics — there are two indissoluble signs: for what she did by herself surpasses what was done privately by any, so far as not to be missed; and what was done when they were on the same footing all together fall short. And indeed in difficulties too she has become superior to the conquerors; for they gave way, but she has been shown to hold out against fortune. Therefore she carries off both victories by no small margin, and conquers
the cities alike in what she achieved and in what she failed.

And indeed she herself has mastered nations and cities at once, but no one has mastered her except with many allies. And further, she has been compelled to war against all together who came against her or stirred against her, while of her adversaries most have held out against a part of her, and few or none have made trial of her power gathered together. So the city of the Athenians has conquered many things many times, yet she herself is, equally, unconquered. And, greatest of all, no one has mastered her — for no one has brought her judgment to terms, but all such misfortunes have been those of an army — while she herself has enslaved the judgments of her adversaries together with their deeds: making Xerxes flee from his affairs as a thing to be prayed for, and laying the Lacedaemonians low — those who heard of it no less than those present in the battles and stumbling. And one might know that the case of these cities is not equal nor alike, either in the greatness of the deeds or in the darings or in anything whatever of their possessions. For the Lacedaemonians, having met misfortune at Leuctra, did not recover, but it was for them like a man's death. For they refused to make peace with the Thebans, thinking it a becoming misfortune to yield to the city of the Athenians alone; but mingled with the rest of the Peloponnesians, they were no more able to save others than they needed the rest to save them — and yet the city sufficed them for the greatest thing, not to be snatched up once for all, as by the onset of a hurricane or some whirlwind. But the city, cheated in the sea-battle at the Hellespont, and stripped of her ships and her walls, and after this using faction within herself, and with the Lacedaemonians doing nothing moderate, took from them, through one man, the rule of the sea, and herself stood at the head of Greek affairs, as though just coming forward from the Median wars. So not only did she bear the reverses of war more nobly than others bore their good fortunes, but also her

troubles at home she so handled that she is a measure of self-restraint for all men, and no one has been able, even later, to find anything better than what was done by them. She showed it both in the overturning of the constitution under the Four Hundred, which she dissolved without a sound, and in the war against the Thirty, which became no greater against more than after those men. And indeed of self-restraint and daring at once no men have brought forth clearer tokens — those who, being a little more than fifty, the first to resolve these things, undertook to risk themselves at once against the dominion of the Lacedaemonians by land and sea and against those in the city itself, thinking they must either live in freedom or not look upon the sun, which had become a witness of cowardice for them. And when they had contended against those from the town, and ranged themselves against the Lacedaemonians, and held the Piraeus, and become for men a pattern of hope in dangers, the people, now gathered together, came at once to blows and well-nigh to words, as though each side would war on behalf of the other, not on its own behalf; so that one could not determine whether it belonged to the enemy to curse the faction, or to the well-disposed to join in praying for the city, since it was dissolved in this fashion. For it sickened by the nature of all men, but was healed by its own; so that this too has brought it emulation rather than misfortune. And I wish to say only this much further about those men: that in daring they surpassed not only the Lacedaemonians, but well-nigh even their ancestors at Marathon. For those, even if far inferior to their adversaries, yet took courage being in a body of considerable number; but these, the whole being a little more than those against whom they fought the tyrants, seized Phyle. And those, while the city flourished, conquered strangers and barbarians; these, when she had fared otherwise, conquered the Lacedaemonians, rulers of the Greeks, and those from the town, their own. And having conquered

their enemies by good courage, they conquered their own people by fairness. Using both — the courage in the contests and, after the deeds, the resolving of what must be resolved — they so recovered the city that, if one wished not to relate everything, one could conceal the misfortune that befell in the war: so did they both choose and accomplish what followed in keeping with the deeds above. And yet, by how great an abundance must one think this city surpasses that one, to which, when she was stripped of all, the Lacedaemonians were so far inferior?

But what is no less worthy than any of their deeds to tell and to honour: when the Lacedaemonians demanded what they had lent the Thirty against the people, then, when they had come to terms, the people paid it off jointly, that they might confirm the compact by deed. And indeed how the Lacedaemonians dealt with one another we could not tell — for they hid it; but the city, besides so settling its own affairs with many witnesses, became a pattern for the rest. The multitude of the Argives, at any rate, when later it sickened, she healed by deed and word; for, sending to them and reminding them of her own affairs, she reconciled them. They appear, then, to have administered alike their own affairs and the common affairs of the Greeks, alone of all; for they thought they must rescue the Greeks not only from enemies, but also relieve them when sick among themselves; and they themselves, prepared both against the wars abroad and against the troubles at home, were seen to be beyond hope. Not, then, that those coming from elsewhere and far younger were arrayed against autochthonous and older men; nor that the city taught others; nor that, though taking forethought for nothing but war, the city won more in other things than in this — not these alone show the inequality, but also that in the very affairs and occasions of war she appears to prevail so far,

whether things go well or otherwise, as the things said make clear and as one may see from what we shall add. For I feel toward the deeds of the city as men feel toward those in their prime: for the deed that ever shows itself appears to me the fairest, and I set this down according to the discourse. These things, then, some god would judge well; but I, as I promised, will go through the most renowned of the rest, from which one may at once reckon the judgment and the power of the city. One war, and a first strange and wonderful one, she undertook on behalf of the Thebans. For when the Lacedaemonians, judging the rest mere play, as though you were exhausted, began their dominion from their own allies and proclaimed a garrison against the Thebans, both things astounded the Greeks; for the city had never used bitterer enemies, nor again had the Lacedaemonians used allies at once more eager and more able against that very city, not only at the beginning and the middle of the war, but even at the last, when it was over. Yet the people did not rejoice at what was happening, nor again blame the inopportuneness in that they had as yet neither ships nor wall; but, as though where the Lacedaemonians moved, there they had to be those who met them, throwing the city into the midst of the dangers of war, beside the very memorials of their misfortunes, they went out to Haliartus against Lysander and Pausanias and rescued Boeotia. And then indeed Lysander exactly perceived that he had not, as he supposed, conquered the city of the Athenians, but had only dreamed, much as children dream; for she had at once recovered from her misfortunes, while he was not administering the affairs of the Greeks, but lay among the rest. And not long after, a penalty Greek and befitting the city overtook the Corinthians too, and these also flee to the city — whom anyone would have guessed, from the circumstances, that, do them whatever harm she might, she could never think she had taken sufficient vengeance; but they, judging concerning these as concerning the Thebans, go to the help of Corinth, as one would on behalf of one's own land; and, the war being

great and continuous at Corinth, having faced danger in front in many battles, and walled them in, and guarded both them and the city through all, they added that noblest thing: for, holding Acrocorinth and being able to seize the city when they wished, they did not take it nor resolve to, showing by deed that they were warring for the cause of those they championed, not doing anything privately for themselves. And at last they brought the Lacedaemonians to such a strait that they take refuge again with the king of the Persians and through him make the much-talked-of peace, giving up the Greeks dwelling in Asia — about whom I make no accusation; but if one should ask them whether they conceded these things willingly or by compulsion, if they shall say willingly, they must say they betrayed them — and who would believe it? but if unwillingly and by necessity, they admit, surely, that they were beaten by the city in the whole; for they would not, if they had any resource in their affairs, have then deliberately taken on such shame. So that, by the only argument left to them, they themselves bear witness that the city then had the advantage in the war — and that no small one. And since I have mentioned the peace, I wish here again to go back a little. For of the two things by which cities are judged, war and peace, and both of these having come to the Greeks against the barbarians, in war the city so excelled that what she alone accomplished is the greatest of the deeds — or, if one set it among the later, she so far surpassed those who shared as if she had contended by herself. And apart from these, she is witnessed by the three occasions: for the first deeds of the war she accomplished alone; in the second, having risked herself in front even against the king, she carried off the prizes of valour; and the last are her own — the sea-battles and land-battles about Cyprus and Pamphylia, and the long course; so that she alone and first conquered the barbarians, and

having joined with others, she conquered her fellow-combatants no less than her adversaries — and she alone remained. But indeed, how great the difference of the peace! For the city's peace lays commands upon the king and says that he too must do what is bidden; for it does not let him sail within the Chelidonian and Cyanean isles, and "if you pride yourself on your cavalry, you shall none the more drive as far as the sea, but you shall keep off the sea," it says, "by a day's ride of the very cavalry, and you shall obey concerning the Greeks alike, both those in Greece and those in your own land." These things the city's peace says; the other says that the Greeks dwelling in Asia shall obey the king, and that he shall do concerning them whatever he wishes, and it has added that he should define what is just for the rest. Is the chief-point equal, or the difference small? Is it not the whole opposite?

Again, the dealings with the Greeks and the resolving of the wars among them. The city, then, sent back with peace the Lacedaemonians she had taken, doing them no harm, as though it were enough to have conquered by virtue; but those of the Lacedaemonians in the Hellespont — for so it is decent to say — whom they took in the sea-battle, the Athenians being outwitted, they slaughtered out of hand; and I add nothing more, and that with the pattern at hand from home, how the city is toward the unfortunate; yet not even so did they imitate it — so far were they from being able to have shown it first themselves. And further, those thought nothing enough, but went as far as the demolition of the walls; while the city, having conquered all the Peloponnesians in the upper times, when she recovered Euboea, did not advance further, but gave back willingly even what she had gained beforehand in the war — Megara, Nisaea, Troezen, Achaea, Pegae. And it seems to me that the matter of the captives, and everything of the kind altogether, is a sign of a twofold virtue in the city, not, as one might say, merely of humanity. For those, I think, with whom such things

succeed beyond hope or power, cling to their present fortune, as those unable to hunt do not let go what is unexpectedly caught, nor, even if one should think fit to ransom it, would they value it at its worth, but, adding their own incapacity, they exact more. But she, I think, conscious that she was the stronger in the whole, never haggled, hoping for what was absent on equal terms with what was present; so she gave back everything to the enemy more easily than they demanded their own. And indeed which single Lacedaemonian mastered the city, not a man could say — where they did not even master her acting in common, alone; while one Athenian man took from the Lacedaemonians the rule of the sea, alone of men having been general at once with the king and for the city — or rather for the Greeks. For doing no wrong whatever to the one who trusted him, he walled the city and freed the Greeks, conquering the Lacedaemonians by island and by city. Now the very rule of the sea the city acquired from her conquests over the barbarians, the natural enemies; they from the city's misfortunes. Having acquired the rule, the one so ordered each thing that he who administered it was called just by the Greeks themselves, alone of the Greeks, on this account, and there is no need of any further symbol of the title which the city then acquired through him; the others so disposed those who gave themselves up that they made the noblest defence of all men on behalf of the charges that arose against the city from some at certain seasons; and the cause was not cruelty, nor what one might say of those readily accustomed to censure, but the not reaching, in their natures, as far as the equal. And indeed the one held their rule more than seventy years, the others did not preserve it even for three Olympiads; so that it truly could not have been otherwise, unless they had received it at the first when the Olympians brought it forward.

These are the very things at which I am vexed when men wish to compare. Perhaps, then, I too seem to some to do an absurd thing — finding fault, yet myself having advanced into the like discourse, and having said the very things for the sake of which I say one ought not to speak. Yet from these very things one would most see that the favour is not wonderful which they think to lay up for the city, nor are such things to be contended for on purpose. So that if anyone thinks fit that these things should be unspoken by us too, well-nigh for this reason it has been said; and apart from this, the speeches have come about without slander and for the sake of the need that fell in the way. For there was no other way to show what I had set out to show, so that out of the very things I was fleeing, from these I was led to speak. For the Lacedaemonians seem to me to feel toward the city what Teucer in Homer feels toward Ajax. For he too, fighting in front of the rest, withdraws to Ajax and through him appears, and likewise is also hidden; and the Lacedaemonians, who excel the Greeks and fight in front in their needs, are to be compared as children to the city. And the proof: of all their possessions and deeds, the greatest are those they have shared with the city; and of these, what they did apart they failed in, but what they did with those from the city they accomplished most gloriously of men. So through the city they are both shown and again hidden. Yet I have been led against my own intention into these speeches, so that I would have wished even the trophies I am about to mention to stand dedicated to the city from others, and that it should not be necessary to add to most of them "from the Lacedaemonians." But as it is, the very facts lead this way, so that it will be said not for the sake of comparison, but that the deeds may not be wholly passed over; for there are some I have left out — and there is need, it seems, of no ordinary course.

They conquered, then, at Lechaeum, and destroyed well-nigh the whole army; they took the forts in Corinth and drove out the Lacedaemonians established there and razed the walls; they went into Arcadia and as far as Laconia, and shut up those in Phlius, and set up a trophy of those who came out against them, and again over the Mantineans and Sicyonians in the plain and over the allies; they sailed along as far as Byzantium, and made the whole region about Thrace their own, and conquered the remaining harmosts and garrisons at Methymna and off Abydos. And they had so great a superiority that they even reconciled the kings of the Thracians. And when the unexpected disaster about the Cadmea took place, they alone of the Greeks kept both the justice of the shameful peace and the noble and truly just things of the Greeks, marching out against the Lacedaemonians — of both of which what greater thing can one say concerning the city? For they conceded the peace last of the Greeks, and not before they knew that they must war not only against the Lacedaemonians and at the same time the king and Seuthes and Dionysius and the Peloponnesians — for against this they were prepared — but also against their own allies; so betrayed were they; and not even so did they endure it with all the votes, but they condemned those who had persuaded them, holding it against their own nature and not lawful that any Greek whatever should consent to obey the king before the trophies. And when, even against this peace, they went into Thebes — of those whose name on such occasions I shrink from speaking — not only first of the Greeks, but also alone, they laid hold of the matters as though seizing a windfall, and displayed not one kind of benefaction, but left out no kind of benefaction: receiving the exiles, and arranging the deed for them and rehearsing it beforehand like a drama in their midst, and giving exemption and citizenship and a share in all things,

as to those who had removed from Corinth and Thasos and Byzantium.
