Then, when there was need also of help through arms, they went out, well-nigh all of them, as though about to share in a procession and not in dangers, imitating their former going-out, and in purpose even surpassing it. For then they went out though they had no alliance with the Thebans; but in these times, even when the pillars about the alliance had been thrown down by the Thebans, yet they did not reckon up their folly against the need, nor were they more angry with those who justly faced danger than with those who unjustly attacked. And, using such brilliant reasoning, they set a fitting end upon it. For they conquered by no small margin, nor so as merely to frighten the Lacedaemonians, but, casting out the garrison and the harmosts under truce, they brought the city back up to its original rank. And this contest they took up on behalf of the freedom of the Thebans; the next, on behalf of their very preservation. For when the Lacedaemonians were spurred on by what had happened, and came on with the whole alliance, they ranged themselves before the city of the Thebans, setting against them generals more fearful to them than those that they furnished with Agesilaus, and becoming through all the saviours of the city. And all sorts of things stand round me, as in a history of those same times, which not only is it not easy to go through all, but not even all of one general in order. Which of them, passing by, shall I mention? The sea-battle at Naxos, so great a deed? Or the contests about Corcyra? Or the things done on the Thracian coast on behalf of the Greece there? Or those in Acarnania? Or those everywhere? Or, leaving aside all the rest, shall I tell that which I hold greatest and most wonderful and alone truly worthy of the Athenians to have done — that, when the Thebans, having mastered the Lacedaemonians at Leuctra, planned to destroy them, and

matters had been left in such a state for the Lacedaemonians that either some hand of a god had to be held over them, or the city had to inherit the dangers that were theirs, willingly — and yet a herald had come at the very beginning from the Thebans, crowned as for good tidings, and the whole Peloponnese had come, giving itself up, bidding them lead for the destruction of Sparta, and threatening, if not, to join the Thebans — yet they, at the herald's words, so wept as though hearing of some misfortune of their own, and sent him off as one come from the barbarians, cheated of his hope most utterly; and they chose the desolation of the Lacedaemonians instead of the voluntary alliance of the Peloponnesians and the friendship of the conquerors, not remembering what they themselves had suffered, but thinking it their own business to dissolve what the Lacedaemonians would suffer if overlooked. And what is most worthy of admiration in their nature, and to be reckoned greater than human: for, when it was possible for them to have the Lacedaemonians follow them both by land and by sea, or to overlook them thrust headlong down — allies, perioikoi, household slaves, all risen up — they received them on equal terms; and when the power of the Thebans was advancing like a flame against the city of the Lacedaemonians and the rest of the Peloponnese, they alone, of Greeks and barbarians, standing in front, prevented it. From which they were so regarded by all that the city became the council-chamber of the whole alliance.

I marvel, then, at those who dare to bring forward against the city the cases of the Melians and Scionaeans — where on earth or sea are they when they make these accusations? Have they heard only these of the deeds of the city of such a character, or would they not have wished both these and all else that belongs to the city to belong to their own fatherlands? For if they shall say they would not wish it, let them show in turn what they pride themselves on; but if they would not flee the choice, were some god to offer it them, let them stop putting their hand to arguments greater than themselves. And further,

do they accuse the city or what befell? For if the city, they know nothing, it seems, of the greatest things, but the things by which the city is known have escaped them; and if they blame what befell, then, thinking the things the city chose unlike the others, they so blame her that, out of the very things by which they disparage the matter, they praise the city. For then the wickedness of a city or of a private man is shown, when either the blameworthy things alone belong to one, or when one convicts him of more or greater bad things than fair ones — let it be added. But when, examining through all, one finds one and two, you are, without knowing it, praising by what you let pass — especially if you make the judgment not even of a private man, but of a city, and that the oldest of the Greek cities, and the one to which most of what is fitting has befallen. But if one must answer about these too, I will not say how those who later were able dealt with these very same matters; for I have not set out to grieve any of the Greeks, but the discourse is dedicated to the race of the Greeks as a common ambition; nor, if I show others having done greater and more terrible things, is this a defence on behalf of the city, but rather a confession taking refuge in pardon; I have no need, then, of such a defence. But it seems to me that those who bring forward such arguments have altogether been ignorant of the nature of affairs, and dwell, as it were, outside the inhabited world. For how could one say they reason moderately about realities, or how they ought to discourse about empire, if they have first been ignorant of this — its nature? For all empire, surely, belongs to the stronger and is contrary to the very law of equality; or else, how is it equal, or where is it just, either to levy tribute from another's land, or to lay laws on those who need none, or to judge their affairs, or to command, or to make war, or to acquire what does not belong to one? For in general none of these things

comes about on terms of equality. So that if anyone is precise about justice and wishes to be a sophist rather than to concede to the nature of things, he might as well strike out simply all rule and power; for all these things are within the law of the stronger. Then, out of wisdom, let him go up as far as the gods, refuting, and saying that not even these deal with men on equal terms, but have chosen to be stronger. But, I think, these are the views of men worthy of a corner and who have not seen the sun, which takes from the other stars the power to shine. And if it is necessary that such things attend all dominion and all abundance, and this is the law of empire — not to be judged on equal terms with the subjects — then let one go off victorious when he has shown that any whatever of the other powers, whether Greek powers or barbarian kingdoms, used a smaller measure of advantage-taking than one can find with the people of the Athenians. For she will appear, in what she deliberated with surpassing nobility, to have used the character of one man, the best; and in what some bring as charges, not to have erred against the common nature of men, but to have followed the necessity of empire — and, by power having become ruler at the first, by humanity, fearing the burden of empire, to have willingly let it go, and well-nigh to have herself become the cause of the charges against her. For having used, toward all, the greatest commonness and moderation, and in a way having made men sharers rather of the constitution than holding them down by the law of dominion, she suffered the same as the kindly among masters; for it was not for her other fairness that she got thanks from some, but if she compelled anything, she conspicuously seemed to use force. And indeed, if she appears to have done these things to men holding the rank of subjects, let us grant it to those who wish to slander; but if to those who had revolted and outraged her beyond their desert, and to those who were openly enemies — which of the two is it worth accusing? I think those who furnished the necessity; since those men too seem to me, as if having this very thing as a pledge,

to have been exalted, and, trusting most in this, to have erred — not in thinking they would master the city through to the end, but in thinking that, even if taken, they would suffer nothing terrible, since the Athenians are by nature savers. And it is plain: for the things they changed their minds about concerning the Mytilenaeans — what city can conquer with what she resolved at the first? For what those decided on the first day belonged to the judgment, and to the wrongs they had suffered; what they changed their minds about on the next day belonged to the city alone, and the trireme had overtaken the trireme. And I marvel if all men honour the defence of private men made by deed, while the solemn ones do not see by what and how great deeds the city has defended herself concerning these matters. And of sun and moon we do not accuse what harm they do, but admire of what goods they are the causes; yet shall we judge the city by the things in which she offended some, and not by those in which she dealt with all, nor from her whole nature? I think not. As though one should accuse the gods of the thunderbolts and the thunders, and if anything be shaken, neglecting to consider their whole and common benefactions. The city, then, made the Scionaeans homeless, but saved all the Greeks both in common and severally — and that ten thousand times. And I would gladly inquire of those who lightly think fit to accuse themselves of such great matters, whom they say she made homeless such as she prevented the Thebans from being made homeless, or whose walls she razed such as she set up for the Corinthians, or whom she destroyed such as the Lacedaemonians and the cities with them whom she preserved — by many other ancient and noble deeds, and at the last by the cavalry-battle about Mantinea, the best of the Greek ones, and, I think, of those that are remembered.
But what is, as it were, the chief-point of those times, and what set the seal upon all the city's deeds, both the earlier and those of that time —

for when Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily and ruler of many of the cities in Italy too, conceived the design of attacking Greece, weakened by the length of her wars — partly having long courted the barbarians neighbouring the Greeks, partly calling in the king of the Persians, and the matter now coming to a boil — two Athenian generals checked the attempt: the one taking all the ships sailing in from Sicily, men and all; the other defeating the Lacedaemonians at sea off Leucas and making the sea his own. For she alone of cities did not bring in a tyrant, did not admire wealth, did not security, did not exchange pleasures for justice, but, as one made by nature to live for all, so she conducted herself. And accordingly all who desired the rule of the Greeks spent their lives warring against the city. And Philip overlooked the rest of the Greeks, and some he persuaded by hopes and gifts to work with him; but against the city he continued warring from the beginning, as though filling out some necessary boundary. And she, so long as she was able, rescued some, and to others stood in the place of a fatherland, and, like a mother, toiled in advance for all on behalf of her children, and alone preserved the symbol of Greece and overshadowed the misfortunes that then held it; but when matters declined, there was nothing in Philip's way, and it was clearly shown that both the victories of the city are the victories of the Greeks, and the reverses of the city are the reverses of all the Greeks. For they did not give up the leadership to Philip before the city accepted the peace. And though I have much of the later times to tell, and strange battles and wonderful darings and extraordinary endurances, I no longer see the occasion sufficing. So much only I will add to the discourse about these things and have done: four wars, to divide them by kind, the city has made — some her own

private wars, some on behalf of the common cause of Greece, some on behalf of those who in turn asked her help; and among these very suppliants are some by whom she had been wronged and against whom she had charges from before. I say, then, that this one figure of war by itself convicts all the Greek deeds together of being later. For more are those whom the city, after they had behaved senselessly toward her, saved, than those whom she remembered with resentment though they had rather done her good — I mean the Thebans from the Lacedaemonians, the Corinthians from the Lacedaemonians, the Lacedaemonians from the Thebans, the Euboeans from the Thebans, when she brought forth tokens of a twofold virtue, preserving for some their cities and the land of which she had been deprived by them, and releasing under truce those whom she had conquered; again the Euboeans from Philip, the Byzantines, the Perinthians, the Chersonesites, the Chalcidians on her own part, and ten thousand others. In return for which, if one had to make an image of the city, as of a private man, it would befit the Athenians' alone, and to be honoured like a common statue of Greece. For what the prytaneion is to the city, this the city has become to all the Greeks in common in their needs, ever furnishing themes fairer than the trophies and the inscriptions.

But what has been done apart from dangers, and yet no less than any shows what the affair of the Athenians ever was, escaped us in the earlier discourse, but now perhaps it is no worse to render. For when a compact had been made by them with the Lacedaemonians — that, if they mastered the barbarians, they should destroy those who had medized — when the dangers had passed, they forgot the enmity. And the Lacedaemonians, set on doing what had been resolved, they prevented, seeing the multitude of the cities by which Greece was going to be made smaller; so that not only to the common race of the Greeks, but even to those who from the beginning had erred both against herself and against the Greeks, the city was ever, at some time, of profit, and whatever she conquered she conquered exactly on behalf of all.

And about these things enough. But what no one, so far as we know, has until now mentioned in the common praises, this I will not cease until I have said. For, just as it seems to me not lawful, when one adorns deeds with speeches, to pass over the mention of the part that concerns speeches themselves. For alone of all men, as the saying goes, you have set up a bloodless trophy — not over Boeotians, nor over Lacedaemonians, nor Corinthians, but over all your kindred — I mean, not as one would name Greeks set in distinction against barbarians, but over the common race of mankind — and you have won an honoured and great victory for all time, not like the disputed battle at Tanagra, nor, by Zeus, like that at Marathon, which conquered so greatly, but truly the one befitting man, and lasting, and which it is pious to call a child of Zeus. For all the cities and all the races of men have inclined toward you and your way of life and your tongue. And the power of the city is not held together by garrisons stationed about, but because all on purpose have chosen your ways and adopt themselves, so far as possible, into the city, praying that both their children and themselves may have a share of the noble things among you. And neither do the pillars of Heracles hinder, nor are these things bounded by the hills of Libya, nor again by whichever Bosporus you will, nor by the straits of Syria and Cilicia, but over all the earth, by some divine fortune, there comes an emulation of your wisdom and your custom, and all men have held this one tongue to be the common tongue of the race; and through you the whole inhabited world has become of one tongue. And you would see charioteers and herdsmen and those who live by the sea and all the nations, whether by cities or by countries, holding fast to your tongue and trying to lay hold of the soil, like those unable to swim. This testimony I say, men of Lacedaemon

and all Greeks — and from yourselves and from the foremost among you in particular — is paid to the city still now, every day, of her victory; for they have abandoned their ancestral tongues, and would be ashamed even to converse among themselves in the old speech with witnesses present; but all have come to this one, thinking it a kind of boundary of culture. This I call the great empire of the Athenians — not two hundred triremes, or more, nor Ionia, nor the Hellespont, nor the Thracian coast, which has changed ten thousand rulers. For so great was the difference of these speeches from all others from the beginning, and it was made still more manifest in time, that not only, when the others have well-nigh died out by now, do these so flourish, but one might even say that all the speech of the others — and not only of barbarians, but of the Greeks themselves — resembles the babblings of stammering children, compared with that which comes from you. For up to two or three words one might listen and be pleased, as in a game; but for the rest there is already surfeit, and everything is found wanting; but this alone is proportioned to all festivals, to all assemblies and council-chambers, and besides suffices for all occasions and places and is equally becoming; for it alone, well-nigh, possesses the two first things, I mean solemnity and grace. And indeed, of the contest through all, and the strain and the running and the mastery, who could come near, bringing another tongue, and not depart truly like a child beaten by a man — that I may put it becomingly? For all poetry from you is the best and most perfect, both whatever excels in solemnity and whatever in graces. And if one must mention Homer too, the city shares in this ambition as well, not only through the colony-city, but because his speech too is plainly from here. And all the kinds of prose among you are the best, and those which the men from you composed; and well-nigh all who have conquered through all among the Greeks have conquered

by the power of the Athenians. And if there is anything in our own case too — this is now, the gods being gracious — this also refers to you, so that one cannot convict the speeches of being foreign; for, as though nature had foreseen from the beginning how far the city would surpass the rest in deeds, she furnished her speeches worthy of it, that she might both be adorned by her own goods and, if she should need any of the others, have this too to give along with the rest. Before, then, you saved those of the Greeks who fled to you; but now you simply uphold all men and all races by the fairest of benefactions, becoming leaders of all culture and all wisdom, and purifying all men everywhere. For in the Eleusinian rite you are called, for those who come, interpreters of the holy things and guides of the mysteries; and through all time you stand, for all men, the interpreters and teachers of the sacred offerings brought into the midst. In return for which you draw all men with fitting incantations — not stirring them with the charm-wheel, but with the fairest of remedies, with speech, which the gods gave to man alone of all creatures as worth all things. So that the other cities, which each men honour, they would, I think, place after their own fatherland; but in the case of the Athenians it is reversed, and all would say they honour not yours after their own, but their own after yours, as this being the one truly their own and prior — and not a single one would feel envy. For just as it is the custom to honour the gods even before parents, as being the common parents and benefactors of all, so it is pious to honour the common fatherland of the race before one's own.

It is fitting, then, to tell also how great is the reverence that is and has been from all toward this city, and through all times always. For not only when Greece flourished was she thought worthy of the first place, but also in the changes there is none that has come to be equal to her. For Philip, prospering by the battle of Chaeronea, at once seized the city of the Thebans with a garrison, but the city of the

Athenians he did not even endure to look upon, but stood in his place out of reverence for the stronger. And I am silent about Alexander, how he was ever deferential toward her. And the present empire of land and sea — may it be immortal — does not refuse to adorn Athens in the rank of teachers and nurturers, but so great is the abundance of honours that the city now fares as differently as she does not occupy herself with affairs. And the rest of her happiness is well-nigh like to what it was in those times when she held the rule of Greece — both in revenues and in precedence and in what has been conceded by all. And, most beloved of the gods of all: when the affairs of the Greeks flourished, she continued conquering both Greeks and barbarians; but in those things in which alone she seemed to have the worse in the later times, from these she came off so much more nobly and more fortunately in the end, that the cities of those others have perished, and such as are left are led by the law of empire and are subject as tributaries to tribute and the other necessities; but she was not so much diminished then, nor for so long a time, as, from then and through so long, she has been honoured up to this day, not only before those, but before all the others. And it is plain: for no one would take pride in Pella as his fatherland, nor in Aegae; but there is no Athenian of the Greeks who would not rather have been born a citizen of the existing city. And not only do private men thus prize Athens, but also the cities — those truly founded from here and by you — would more gladly say they are from you than acquire power equal to yours; and others go round in a circle, seeking somehow to trace themselves back to you. And indeed there is memory of five empires — and may there not be more; of these, in that of the Assyrians, the oldest, are the first deeds of the city, and whatever of the divine matters falls within this time; in the second the city was being raised up; the third she conquered through to the end; in the fourth she alone held out, and came off best

of the others. And in the all-best and greatest, the one now established, she holds the precedence of all the Greek world, and has so fared that one would not easily join in praying that she should have the ancient state in place of the present. And one might know how much the city excels through all the ages, if, taking her possessions — all of them perhaps not possible, or rather plainly impossible, but such as can be — and dividing them, assigning one to this country and city, another to that, one should then make a contest of the discourse, as of poets or choruses; for I do not think one would easily find the winner: as if one should pride herself on having first borne the race of men, another on having first shown the crops, another on having shared with most, another on having revealed laws, another festivals, another on lying among the fairest of land and sea at once, another on glorying in the goods of wisdom, another reckoning up the deeds in wars, another how many of the Greeks she received, another the colonies she sent out, another whatever of the city's possessions one might give her — I say that thus it would most become manifest by how great a superiority the city has surpassed the rest for you. For what suffices Greece when divided, this she alone has all together. And so, as in all things she has so great an abundance, so again in each she glories in many that bear toward the same point.

For instance, of the divine matters, at once two are first and greatest, the honour from the gods and the zeal toward the gods. And again, of the honour from the gods, should one tell of the visits, by which they honoured the community, or the nurtures, by which they reared those in office like their own children? Or the trials they held? And of the trials again, those they held against one another concerning the city, or those in the city against one another about their

differences, or those held here mingled, with heroes and gods, with gods as judges? And of the gifts likewise it is not easy to find the greatest. Let city contend with city about these too — the one bringing the crops of Demeter, the other those of Dionysus, and these not only from the vine, but of the other cultivated fruits; let the third tell of the gift of Athena, and that twofold; is it not enough, when the gifts from the gods are divided among many cities, for each to pride herself as having the fairest? Again, the things toward the gods: on the one hand the temples, on the other the yearly sacrifices and processions, of which some came to be first among you, others to a surpassing degree still even now. And the unspoken rites, in which those who share seem to have their affairs better even after the end of life — who would not say it enough to set against all one thing? But indeed, of converse with men, what mode of benefaction has it escaped? First, the sharing of the crops; next, the other sharing of the rites; third, the championship in the wars; fourth, the help ever coming from wisdom to all, both for private houses and for the common affairs of cities. And of wisdom itself, shall we tell of the laws, which most still use, your laws, or of the discourses? And of the discourses, those concerning rhetoric, or the dialectical, or poetry, or the rest of prose — or, if you will, what kind of poetry? For whatever you name first or last belongs to the city as the first.

Consider, then, the matters of war too: on the one hand the private contests, on the other those on behalf of others; and again the successes at home, and again likewise those abroad, against Greek and barbarian alike; and which will you tell of, the courage or the humanity that is present in the very wars? For as in one spring all that you divide flows together again into one another and mingles — into the benefactions both the wars, by the need of those who asked, and

the goods from wisdom; and into the wars again both the private and those on behalf of those who asked. Again, then, of the wars, whether on their own behalf or on behalf of others, must one tell the sea-battles, or the land-battles, or the horse-battles, or the wall-battles? For in all these the city is supreme. Or, if you will, which of her deeds at sea is greatest, or which by land? Let three boundaries, then, be set for her, by which, if not herself, yet at least the rest she has indisputably surpassed: of land-battle, that at Marathon; of sea-battle, that at Salamis; of horse-battle — I am at a loss which to judge, but let it be that at Mantinea; of wall-battle no one has ever even disputed. And shall we set it down by the multitude of the trophies, or by the greatness of the deeds? Or how shall we render the worth? So both through all and through each she conquers in many ways. For she has made the most and greatest contests, and on behalf of the fairest things; and the most and fairest trophies are from Athens; and the most and fairest discourses, surpassing through all, are those of this city; and I will add, from here too the wisest and keenest and safest and most just generals, and more than all the Greeks together. And, to say it as a chief-point, by these three things the life of men is fulfilled: by abundance of necessaries, by the noble things of culture, by the equipment for war; for of the two seasons, peace and war, the one is common to both, one is set aside for the season of peace, and one makes men able to defend what they have. Of these, then, let whichever one wishes be greatest; and let it be granted that these belong to three cities, each to each: I say, then, that by whichever of them one judges, the conquering belongs to the city. For she will appear to have shown all and advanced in all things to the utmost; so by all the

judges she conquers, and over all the countries besides; so that one would not hesitate to say that she must be proclaimed first and second and third among the Greeks, as in the chariot-races — if indeed the chariot too is anciently from Athens, not from Sicily. Well, let these things be as they are.

But the matters of her greatness and her other equipment — who would not say they are worthy of her whole fortune and of the great name of the Athenians? On the one hand the very circuit of the town, the greatest of the Greek towns and the fairest anywhere. And I am silent about the walls that once came down to the sea, a day's road in their whole length, and other circuits by the sea answering to those about the city. But the demes one may surely behold, some of which are more splendidly furnished than cities elsewhere; and all the ornament, both from nature and from art, rivalling both in the city and in the country. Of the natural things, this air, choice out of much, and so many harbours, each one worth many. And further, the very position of the acropolis, and that which strikes one everywhere as gracious, like a breeze. And what is worthy of note in these very things: for other cities, however they may stand as to climate, are tolerably outdone by their own country; but, though the air of all Attica is thus, the air over the city is the best and purest. And one might know her from afar by the air over her head, as by a kind of radiance.

And the things from nature are such, with much of what exists left out. But of the things of art, what should one set greatest, or what tell first? For the temples here are the same — the greatest and fairest anywhere — and statues, apart from the heavenly ones, the first of the first art, both old and new; and besides these, treasuries of books such as nowhere else on earth

plainly, and very much a proper ornament of Athens, and, as befits the present license and manner of living, baths surpassing in solemnity and luxury, and race-courses and gymnasia; so that, if one should take away from the city the Erichthonii, the Cecropes, the things of myth, the things of the crops, the trophies on land and sea, the discourses, the men — all the things through which she has passed her age — and should consider her like the cities that now pride themselves on themselves, she would suffice to conquer by the things that are seen. And indeed some she has had, others she has, and she has neither been robbed of the memory of the things in which she excelled, nor again has she been left behind in her present happiness, if anyone cares to recall these too; but she alone of cities conquers her old things by the old, her new by the new, or, if you will, her old by the new and her new by the old — by her own, I mean, the things of others. And one might see her surpassings from this too: for all who have shared even some small part with the city pride themselves as the best of the rest; but she falls short of no ambition of any whatever, and has no one to share her own through to the end. For instance, the Argives think fit to be the oldest of the Greeks — so too the city of the Athenians; and altogether the old things of the Argives are not like those of the Athenians, nor would a single common judge say so. The Arcadians are autochthonous — after the Athenians, that is; and they are again conquered in the second things, by the discovery and gift of the crops. And it is plain from the Greeks bringing their first-fruits hither, not there. The Lacedaemonians are best in the matters of war — but so too the city of the Athenians; and at any rate the second place is set among them in ambition. The birth of the gods is a grace and honour to Thebes; of these, the one revealed his gift in Attica, and the other the Athenians first of the Greeks led in as a god, apart from the fellowships toward him through Theseus.

But indeed all remember the last strength of the Thebans — of this the city is the cause, and when she had to do the opposite, she did not fear. One might praise the Corinthians for justice; the city, then, has not only wished what is just, but has continued to arbitrate for the rest. The most renowned of all are the contests throughout Greece; and of these the oldest is that of the Panathenaia, or, if you will, that of the Eleusinia. Then the city's gift sets them all in motion — I mean, surely, the city's gift from Athena. The Samothracians glory in their rites, and these are the most named of all, except the Eleusinian; but Delos too is dedicated to the gods — and it belongs to the city. And the very fact that the road to Delphi is a work of the city, and that the Pythian mission is ancestral to the Athenians alone — what could you say but that all these things belong to the gods, who wish in every way to honour Athens and to lay the city's hand, as it were, on all the fair things? And further, there are some of the cities in Asia that pride themselves on the size of their temples, others on the construction of baths better than the need; and these things belong to the city to excess, as though she had been settled but lately. And the fairest thing: for what the rest are zealous to show in statues, of these you possess the temples and the theatres. Statues are admired, and of these too it prevails that the first is yours in the city — apart from the fact that the rest everywhere too belong, in a way, fittingly to the city. For of all the best things, it seems, she is the fatherland, and the leader of all wisdom and art, so that she surpasses not only in her statues, but in her statue-makers themselves.

But indeed, of the seven men — that we may not pass this over either — who became renowned for wisdom, one was from the city; and of the two best lawgivers, the one was this very man. And we have received that to two men of old a vote was given from the gods — to Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian and to

Socrates, who was from you; so that the city shares both in the ambition over common matters and in that over the highest, and there is none of the renowned to whom the name of Athens is not attached. If, then, one should ask which of the law-courts among the Greeks is most honoured and most holy, all would say that on the Areopagus. And what customs did men use most common and most popular? Those of the city of the Athenians, alike for Athenians and for all — one must say, if they are willing to tell the truth. And to demonstrate it through all needs much discourse and time; but you alone of all men held these three customs: to speak each year, at the burials, praises of those who had died on behalf of the city, and to rear their children at public expense until manhood, and then to send them off to their ancestral homes with full panoply; and to rear at public expense the incapable among the citizens. So that, honouring both ability and inability, you showed how each was fitting. And whence are decrees more brilliant or more humane? Of these the ones contained in what has been said I omit, but let one stand for me as a sample, so to speak, for the whole discourse about these things — the decree that prevailed against Arthmius of Zeleia; whom, when, serving the king, he brought gold into the Peloponnese, they voted an enemy of the people of the Athenians, both himself and his line, and dishonoured. And yet the things of all the others together fall short of this one alone. And embassies — most she received, and most she sent out. And whether this is altogether agreed, well; but if not, by the addition it becomes greater, for she sent out most on behalf of those in need. Now all the embassies by which she either persuaded the Greeks in common from time to time not to war with one another, or, sending out, consoled those in need, it is necessary to leave out for their multitude. But here too of two

I will make mention: for she stopped the Argives from faction among themselves, and reconciled the Cretans warring with one another. And of piety together with gentleness and high spirit, what fairer token could one tell? For when the Corinthians once voted not to receive the sacred mission from here at the festival, and even by an embassy forbade the city to send it, they adorned the envoys and the hoplites together and sent them out; and when they were at Eleusis, the Corinthians came making terms, and they sent the mission and brought the hoplites back. And indeed of the mysteries, some have been honoured as ancient, some as necessary, some as known to most. By all the votes the Eleusinia bear off the prize. And about the rest the discourse is not ours; but you alone of the Greeks hold each year a festival no meaner than any quadrennial one, and you receive at the Eleusinion more than others receive in their whole city; and all ever vie to make the present feast conquer in throng of men. But indeed Heracles and the Dioscuri all surely hold to be gods; and to these, while they consorted with men, the city first of all strangers shows the rites; so that those to whom we now do sacred rites, she is plainly the one who made them objects of worship. And of contests of the first rank this one city still now holds the most of all. And, to put it shortly, all things either are among you alone, or are also from you, and one of three things has come about: for some things began from you, others are fairest among you, others most in number. There are, then, some who, having nothing plain to show or to tell of their own deeds, nor anything on which they might justly pride themselves, take refuge in the Trojan times and dispute over ambition — not even so saying anything common to themselves, but hanging upon the glory of one man — like the Phthiotians and Pylians and Ithacans, like certain land-paupers making themselves out through one of the rich. But the city, besides

needing no such refuge, is not deprived of this seasoning either. But the common poet of the Greeks, in the catalogue of the ships and cities, says that the Athenian general came to the height in marshalling "horses and shield-bearing men." And, what is worth more and pure of praise: the others whom he praises, he praises according to the condition of the body, or in some other way as best, as it may chance, of the Achaeans, or of the so-and-so; he says at any rate "of themselves and of the horses that followed the Atreidae," and elsewhere he says, speaking of those then before Ilium, that one was best in archery. And Nestor says to certain of the brilliant men of his own day, "for already in time past I have consorted with better men than you" — and next he counts off many, as being again like to one another and none conspicuously surpassing them. But of Menestheus the poet uses no such addition, but, cutting away all these things at one stroke, says, "to him no man yet upon the earth was like." And a little above these things he tells of Erechtheus, how the goddess reared him, but the earth bore him. So perhaps it is not unfitting that the others, whom he defined as best in each kind with an addition — either of times or of races — he proclaims as themselves; but the one whom, of those sprung from the earth itself, he praises as best, this one he praises as best of all who have sprung in the earth. And again, setting down two of the Achaeans best in the matters of war, he means, surely, by the one of them the namesake from Salamis. And this too, surely, is told as a solemn thing concerning the constitution of the Lacedaemonians, that the god arranged their laws at the beginning; but this same god is plainly seen to have divided the tribes for the city and the clans, and to have ordained for each the fitting sacrifices, just as also he defined for them kings and magistrates and well-nigh the whole rest of the constitution. So that the god would be no less the lawgiver of the city than of them.

And I wish to make mention also of the constitution itself, briefly, so far as I am able; for all praise it, but no one well-nigh has searched out all that is in it. And I call it both simple and not simple. For of the three constitutions — to divide them at the highest — by whichever one would set it down, one sets the city. For at the beginning she will appear to have used kingships, for not a few generations, not only of the Erechtheidae, but of those later who were shown worthy; and democracy, again, both known to a child and the purest and greatest of all, is the one that has come to be among you. And indeed, looking to the council from the Areopagus, I think all would say that one could not take a fairer image of aristocracy, nor one that better preserves the name. So all the patterns of constitutions have started from here; for, as though legislating for men, that each should choose what suits his own ways, so she discovered all and set them forth in common, helping nature everywhere — which we show her to have done with respect to the crops and many other things too. And what is greater still and more perfect: the kings themselves will appear to have loved community beyond the others, and to have set themselves, most of all, on equal terms in their judgments toward the many; and the people, if it found anyone among the many surpassing, willingly set him over itself and used him as a continuing ruler, and kept this same custom toward the few too, if it perceived them better than the rest, but rivals among themselves; and likewise the council, ever looking to how it might make the people greater, and never reckoning its own advantage privately, but judging this both a fair and a real advantage for itself — to stand, with good repute, for the safety of the many. So that reasonably the city is of good repute beyond all the others not only in each constitution, but also in the blending of constitutions, in the

city's case. For just as this whole universe, I think, was composed of four elements, as the old saying goes, and each of these itself again shares by nature in the rest, but by its excess each kind has taken its name apart, so too the constitutions, even if they happen to be most of all distinct, naturally share somehow in one another, if indeed we are to see a kingship upright and just, or likewise a rule of the few or of the many. And one might know it, if one looked at the kingships in the city against the kingships somewhere else of the same times, whether of Greece or of the barbarians; and again the democracy at Athens against the democracies of others; and indeed the council's body against those that are sovereign and ruling somewhere else. For if one must, leaving the rest, speak about the democracy alone, all who have shared in this form will appear, in their wishes and desires, far more headlong and insolent, but in dignity and brilliance not even near to those born of the city. And indeed this the city first showed — not to set store by wealth nor to admire it. For she never exalted those who excelled in property, but thought she owed them only so much from herself as not to be wronged on this account; nor to those surpassing in virtue but inferior in money did she ever anywhere assign less — thinking it shameful, I suppose, that, while of household slaves men reckon best not the wealthiest but the most faithful, of free men, who claim that their worth is defined by money, it should be money and not what each man himself is, that he should be reckoned. And accordingly she alone of cities did not alter the ordinance, nor make what is by nature third first by law; nor, as one may see some of those who profess to philosophize speaking so about these things but in deed falling under and ever conceding to those whom they perceive more powerful — but she, both leading into office and

trusting and judging worthy of all honours, was seen to honour not those of the greatest assessments, but the most decent in their natures; holding that whoever conquers in the account of virtue conquers in all things. And she showed it not least when she was strongest. For when there were at the same times conspicuous men among her — some of them wealthy beyond the first of the Greek houses, others as poor as could be — for the championship of the Greeks she chose one of these latter; and accordingly he won repute by what he was set over, and the city by what it judged. And though there are many things one might say about the constitution, the most are both already taken up beforehand, and the occasion takes them away, and there is no necessity to say all; but adding one thing I will end the discourse about this too. For the fact that the best and that which falls according to license have here coincided, and that the manner of living is most common to all, while the honours are reserved for the most decent — how is this not the mark of a truly free city and constitution, in which it is possible to live as one wishes, but to be honoured and to have power belongs not to those who wish, but to those who have been tested? And accordingly, both in the contests of wars and in their needs, they preserved the fitting thing: they were not zealous about affairs from a half or even a smaller share, but all alike, with their eagerness, vied according to their power, as men contending for a common fatherland and common prizes, and not with risk set before some and lordship, if they prevailed, before others. From which concord and trust of one another flourished throughout the city; and if anywhere they fell into difference, they recognized one another without trouble; but if courage were needed anywhere, all else was folly compared with them — not even all-round athletes who conquer in everything seem to me to prevail so completely in all things. And in what occasions would one not be the better for remembering the city? In campaigns? And whence would one take fairer

examples? Or by what speeches, used, would one better exhort? But in the festivals? But she herself is the leader of these. But in the assemblies and the management of affairs in the city? And what people is itself keener and gentler, or what popular leaders more worthy to admire? But in the practice of speeches and of the rest of wisdom? But even now still all come together here; and the families of the philosophers have not died out, by the good fortune of the city — apart from the fact that those anywhere on earth must of necessity remember at once both speeches and the Athenians, and could never cast from their soul her image, looking into the speeches as into a mirror. And accordingly to all men the name and the soil of the city are so reverend as nothing else, one and the same; and neither private men nor kings honoured her by small things, but so that they themselves gloried in the excesses of the honours they displayed. And plain too is the goodwill and the vote from the very gods, both through the common seer and ancestral interpreter of the city — bidding men to sacrifice the pre-ploughing rite on behalf of the Greeks, and naming her the mother-city of the crops, and further thinking fit that she should wear the crown, as conquering through life. And an eagle in the clouds the god calls her, in comparison with the other townships. To her alone, it seems, of cities the two opposite things have befallen: for both most and fairest things have been said by men about her, and there is none who has obtained fewer. For before all others she has been admired, yet has heard nothing worthy of herself. Before, then, I admired, hearing, the prytaneion of wisdom and the hearth of Greece and the bulwark and all such things that were sung to the city; but now all these seem to me to fall short. But if one must call any city a viceroy of the gods, or kindred to them, or an image and boundary of human nature, this one, I think, would justly be so called.

In return for which, men of Greece, it is fitting neither to feel envy toward the city nor, giving way, to be ashamed, but to increase her from what we have and to share her ambition. For when the Athenians conquer, the conquering is with you. For that all should be best of all is impossible. But as, when a general excels, the city shares in the glory, so, when the leading city is honoured as is fitting, all have a part in the ambition. And I think it brings no shame even to the Athenians themselves, if one offers them their acropolis as ambassador. You too, then, ought, accounting the city as a kind of acropolis or summit of Greece and of your kindred, to adorn her both in deed and in word, and to think that you share in the glory, not that you are robbed of it. The discourse too has been wrought by us as an ornament for the spectacle of the Panathenaia in place of the peplos; and may it be given as a grace of the same goddess to whom both the discourse and the city belong.
